02 / ANALYSIS SETTINGS

Adjust warning sensitivity

Thresholds are starting points. Tune them to your camera and lighting.

What do these numbers mean?

Brightness: 0–255. 0 is black; 255 is white. Higher means brighter, not necessarily better. An overexposed scene can still lose useful information.

Edge detail: no universal scale. Higher means more rapid pixel changes. Low values may indicate blur or a naturally smooth scene. Noise can produce high values.

The sliders set warning cutoffs, not camera settings. Raise a cutoff to warn more often. Lower it to tolerate darker or less-detailed scenes. Nothing here changes camera exposure or focus.

Defaults: brightness 45, detail 60. These are starting values, not validated quality standards.

Set a clear-scene reference

Show a scene you judge well-lit and in focus. Let at least 5 live samples collect, then use the button below. For video, the last 10 analyzed samples must represent a clear scene.

This sets each cutoff to 70% of its median in the latest 5–10 measured samples. It is a convenient starting point, not a learned or validated calibration. Do not use a dark or blurred scene as your reference.

Brightness uses average weighted RGB (0–255). Edge detail uses Laplacian variance at a fixed 320-pixel analysis width. Low detail can reflect blur or a naturally smooth scene.

Read the results at a glance

Start the camera or analyze a video to get an explanation of the latest sample.

100: both measurements meet your chosen cutoffs; it does not guarantee a clear view. 50: the weaker measurement is about half its cutoff. 0: at least one measured signal is zero. Amber means at least one cutoff was missed. A higher cutoff can lower the score without any change in the image.

04 / ENGINEERING NOTES

From pixels to an interpretable signal.

Portfolio research prototype exploring camera-quality observability for surgical-vision workflows. A webcam provides an accessible engineering demonstration; it does not reproduce endoscopic imaging conditions.

01 · Acquire
MediaStream / video file02 · Normalize
320 px wide, preserve aspect03 · Measure
Luma proxy + Laplacian04 · ONNX inference
WASM scoring → telemetry

01 / Photometric signal

Y′ = 0.2126 R′ + 0.7152 G′ + 0.0722 B′
B = mean(Y′)

Weighted gamma-encoded RGB is used as a luma-like proxy, not physical scene luminance. Mean brightness summarizes exposure across the full frame; local dark regions can be hidden by bright areas or specular highlights.

02 / Spatial detail signal

L(x,y) = Y′(x−1,y) + Y′(x+1,y)
+ Y′(x,y−1) + Y′(x,y+1) − 4Y′(x,y)
D = mean(L²) − mean(L)²

Four-neighbor Laplacian variance over interior pixels measures high-frequency detail. Blur can reduce it; sensor noise, texture, and compression can increase it. Analysis width is fixed for more consistent comparisons.

03 / Transparent decision rule

Q = round(100 × min(1, B / Tᵦ, D / Tᴅ))
dark = B < Tᵦ
low_detail = D < Tᴅ

The weaker normalized signal limits the score. Defaults Tᵦ = 45 and Tᴅ = 60 are illustrative and uncalibrated. The ONNX graph executes Div → ReduceMin → Clip → Mul on float32 tensors: metrics [N,2], thresholds [2], scores [N]. Scores are rounded for display. Q is a heuristic, not model confidence or a diagnostic result.

04 / Runtime & resource lifecycle

Vanilla JavaScript ES modules, Canvas 2D pixel extraction, Float64Array grayscale buffer, and a linear-time O(W×H) metric pass. ONNX Runtime Web 1.20.1 executes the scoring graph with a single WASM thread. A startup check requires score 50 for input [90,30] at thresholds [45,60]. Live acquisition requests video only through getUserMedia. Stop camera releases every media track; hiding or leaving the page also stops acquisition.

Live sessions retain at most 3,600 samples, then stop. Raw images are not recorded. File analysis caps work at 20,000 samples. Downloads contain numeric telemetry only.

05 / Real-data evaluation — next step

Create independently annotated clear / dark / blurred / occluded clips. Split by source video or capture session to avoid frame leakage. Tune thresholds on a development split, then freeze them before held-out testing.

Report per-condition precision, recall, false alarms per minute, event detection delay, and performance by camera and lighting. Measure p50/p95 compute time separately from end-to-end delay. No dataset-level results have been measured yet.

06 / Failure modes & next experiment

A sharp obstruction can score highly. Smooth clear scenes can trigger low-detail flags. Auto-exposure, motion, specular reflections, cropping, and sparse sampling can distort results. There is no temporal smoothing or semantic obstruction detector.

A trained softmax classifier now maps the same two metrics to clear, dark, and low-detail labels. It was trained on procedural grayscale scenes, not surgical images. Next: evaluate with independently annotated real footage and investigate richer features or image-based models.

Interview walkthrough

1. Start the camera and show a detailed, well-lit scene. 2. Reduce illumination to inspect brightness changes. 3. Move an object close to the lens to explore detail loss. 4. Adjust thresholds and explain false positives. 5. Stop acquisition and export timestamped telemetry. These manipulations illustrate signal behavior, not validated detection performance.

Implementation references: Camera acquisition / MDN · Media-track lifecycle / MDN. Independent portfolio project; no Andromeda Surgical affiliation or clinical validation is implied.

Built for exploration. Not validated for clinical decisions or surgical guidance. Rule-based scoring and a synthetic-trained classifier run in ONNX Runtime Web. No surgical model validation is claimed.
